rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods <U+2013> three-season (2006/07<U+2013>2008/09) split-plot field experiment at Daxing, NCP, comparing level-basin (BI) and surface drip (DI) irrigation at four scheduling thresholds, three replicates. Q2: Table 4 and Table 9 / Results 'Grain yield and WUE' <U+2013> irrigation amounts measured by flow meter; relative to basin treatment B1, drip treatments D1<U+2013>D4 saved 14, 19, 35 and 35 % of irrigation water with yield decreases of 5<U+2013>22 %; D3 saved 35 % water with 13 % yield loss; conclusions state DI produced expected yields with less water than BI.
rows.notes: Study is a single-site, single-crop (winter wheat cv. Zhongmai 9), plot-scale trial; level-basin irrigation is a surface (flood-type) method, so the comparison fits the passage, though the savings reported (14<U+2013>35 %) are below the 'up to 50 %' figure. Water applied was measured by one method (flow meter); no triangulation. The mechanism for savings (uniform distribution, lower soil-surface evaporation, smaller wetted area) is asserted/assumed (wetted fraction and application efficiency were assumed inputs), not measured, so Q4 is 'no' despite soil water content being monitored. Advantage of DI in yield/WUE is reported mainly under deficit scheduling, but this is an interaction, not stated as a requirement for water saving; economic caveats (investment not considered, wheat and water prices) concern adoption, not the effect. Limitations noted (LAI measurement error on small plots, need for further study of stable soil water) do not address the water-saving result. Water-saving percentages are means without SD/CI; only Duncan letters are given.
